extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and students of scientific method and logic
extracted.subtask_description: Classify and identify common fallacies and prejudices that degrade scientific and philosophical reasoning, with guidance and examples for detecting them (e.g., suppressed premises, a priori assumptions, reification of abstractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Induction, where the facts on which the induction proceeds are erroneous (malobservation, non-observation, or inference from erroneous intermediate marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes errors caused by insufficiently ascertaining the facts on which an induction is grounded, whether the failure be direct malobservation or indirect (mistaking marks for what they are supposed to prove). Treat all inductions whose error lies in faulty ascertainment under this heading. Examples: superstitions founded on mistaken observation; mistaking an uncertain mark for a certain one. Detection tip: verify the empirical facts and the means by which they were obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive fallacies in which the facts are correct, but the conclusion is not warranted by them (overgeneralization from limited or inconclusive evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These occur when true observations are taken to support conclusions they do not in fact justify. Examples include concluding a single cause where multiple causes are possible, or drawing universal laws from inadequate samples. Pay attention to whether the evidence truly establishes the middle term or general law claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Deduction (as classified: fallacies whose premises do not support the conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes of incorrect ratiocination where the premises (though possibly true) do not bear out the conclusion — essentially, vicious argumentation contrary to rules of the syllogism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are cases where the logical form fails: undistributed middle, illicit process, etc. The author notes many apparent deduction-fallacies really reduce to inductive or observational errors once suppressed premises are exposed. Detection tip: make all tacit premises explicit and check syllogistic form; supply suppressed links to see whether premises, if corrected, would support the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies arising from neglect or inability to state the question properly, and to apprehend the evidence with definiteness and precision — confusion being the most obvious characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the place of error is that propositions have not been distinctly conceived or stated (e.g., reasoning in a circle, indistinct premises). Because many links in ordinary argument are tacit, a fallacy may be ambiguous as to its genus. Detection: force the arguer to supply suppressed premises (Socratic interrogation) or, if impossible, judge the most probable suppressed premise; errors often cluster here with others. Example given: arguing from a country's distress to tyranny — the suppressed premise may be false or irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ratiocination (vicious argumentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those deduction-located fallacies in which the premises of the ratiocination do not bear out its conclusion — covered by the rules of the syllogism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the residual class reserved for errors purely of logical consequence (invalid syllogisms). The text emphasizes that once an argument is fully and unambiguously stated, any error will fall into one of the recognized modes; thus make every step explicit and test each syllogistic rule. Where a fallacy can be filled by either a false premise or an unproving (but true) premise, determine which is more likely to have been intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Simple Inspection / A Priori Fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in which no actual inference takes place; propositions are embraced as self-evident or requiring no proof, or because they have intrinsic verisimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers all forms of unjustified 'self-evident' assumptions. The author warns not to attempt to catalogue what may be legitimately accepted a priori, but to note that many unjustified assumptions take the form of treating ideas or intuitions as objective facts. Detection: require empirical support where possible and beware appeals to supposed intuition as sufficient proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking subjective laws for objective laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Tacit assumption that the order among ideas in the mind must obtain among objects in nature: properties of our ideas or their relations are taken to be properties of external things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes taking what is true of conceptions (ideas) as true of reality (e.g., if two things are thought together they must exist together). Examples: many superstitions, attributing causality because of mental association. Remedy: separate psychological associations from empirical relations; test objective correlation independently of mental habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming inconceivability implies impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that whatever we cannot conceive as coexisting or as existing at all must therefore be false or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author rejects this: limits of imagination or current experience do not bound natural possibility. Historical examples: antipodes, resistance to Copernicanism, Newtonian objections to action at a distance. Detection: ask whether inconceivability is a limitation of the mind, not evidence about nature; seek empirical or theoretical enquiry rather than dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming what is easily conceived is likeliest true (simplicity bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prejudice that of possible explanations, that which is easiest to conceive (the simplest) is likeliest to be true: 'nature always acts by the simplest means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This heuristic can mislead; historical example: insistence on circular heavenly motion and epicycle complexity. Simplicity is a guide not a proof; check that the 'simple' hypothesis actually fits the facts without ad hoc complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification / Reification of abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency to conclude that where there is a name, there must be a distinct objective entity corresponding to it (e.g., treating 'whiteness', 'Nature', 'Chance' as substances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reification (mistranslating general terms into 'universal substances') produces mysticism and confuses language with ontology. Detection: analyze whether a general term names a class of phenomena or alleges a distinct entity; avoid inferring independent existence from grammatical or conceptual convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Sufficient Reason misapplied (inferring law from lack of objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that because we see no reason why nature should deviate in one way rather than another, it therefore will not deviate — using absence of an a priori objection as proof of a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author calls this fallacious when used to establish laws without experience (example: inferring inertia because there's 'no reason' for motion in one direction rather than another). This often amounts to petitio principii. Remedy: demand empirical demonstration rather than reasoning from absence of an a priori reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceiving mental association as causal connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that because an idea or image leads us to think of another, there is a real causal or necessary physical relation between the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: omens and prognostics (talking of the devil causing sightings), unlucky days causing failure by suggestion. Beware conflating psychological predisposition with objective causal links; test for causal mechanisms and rule out psychological bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection method: supply suppressed premises
rubrics_metrics.description: To detect many fallacies, especially where links are tacit, the silent assumed proposition must be supplied so one can judge whether it is true or proves the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because arguers often suppress steps, expose and articulate the hidden premises (Socratic interrogation). Where multiple plausible suppressed premises exist, choose the one most likely intended or judge which leads to a false premise vs. an unproving premise. Example: 'distress of country → government is tyrannical' requires either a false universal premise or an irrelevant conditional; clarify which is assumed.
